title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
claim: Per-component scaling metadata dominates compressed adaptor description length; sharing one global scale shrinks it and yields tighter certified bounds.
layout: 2 panels: left method/contrast diagram top-to-bottom, right bar chart; dashed row separators
description: A two-part figure. The left rounded panel is split into three rows by dashed lines. The top row shows LoRA-T adaptation of a frozen pre-trained weight tensor W0, with blue frozen and orange trainable blocks: U, Σ, vectors v times projections P, summed (⊕) and fed to Vᵀ. The middle row, 'Quantisation Scale Choices', contrasts per-tensor scales (red label, a grid of z-to-s mappings for each layer, 'Many scales, high overhead') with a single global scale s* (green label, LoRA-GT ours, 'Single scale, low overhead'). The bottom row is an arrow chain: lower overhead → shorter description length → tighter non-vacuous PAC-Bayes bounds. The right panel is a bar chart of risk for LoRA, LoRA-XS, -TN, -TT and LoRA-GT (green). Blue bars show 0-1 loss and orange bars show Brier loss, with hatched test error and dotted random-baseline lines. The bars shrink toward LoRA-GT.
caption: Compression yields tight, non-vacuous PAC-Bayes guarantees for safety oversight models. Left: LoRA-T with per-tensor versus shared global scaling (LoRA-GT), which removes the per-layer quantisation-scale metadata that dominates PEFT adaptor description lengths under aggressive compression. Right: certified bounds and test risk on BeaverTails under $0$--$1$ and Brier losses, where LoRA-GT achieves the tightest certificates among the shown adaptors while retaining competitive test risk.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.
